en: *An Abridged Exposition of the Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, Scroll One, composed by the Śramaṇa Tanka of Jiankang.
In order to explain this treatise, it shall be analyzed according to three sections: first, clarifying the intent of its composition; second, revealing the [treatise’s]... [text truncated]
Thesis. Third, explaining the meaning of the treatise.
First, regarding the intent of its composition:
The four meanings and eight causes according to the treatise are explained in detail below;
here, they are summarized and condensed into two meanings.
The first is to cause one to depart from delusion.
The second is for the purpose of revealing the truth.
These two each have two aspects: first, the intrinsic; [second, the extrinsic].
Second, regarding others:
the fundamental nature of the minds of all sentient beings is neither moving nor still, neither arising nor ceasing, neither pure nor defiled.
Due to being perfumed by ignorance, it moves and becomes deluded thought.
They transmigrate through birth and death, undergoing all manner of suffering.
Now, I cause sentient beings to realize that the nature of their own minds is originally quiescent and extinguished,
so that they may remain free from the movement of thought.
All that moves is the movement of thought arising from ignorance;
yet ignorance itself has no point of origin.
One who knows the mind to be unmoving and does not give rise to thoughts accords with and realizes the source of the mind, forever free from the cycle of transmigration.
This refers to what is taught in the sutras: attaining the noble wisdom of self-realization by departing from the false appearances of one's own mind.
This is the essential tenet taught in the *Dharmaparyāya* Sūtra;
by relying on that which has been thoroughly realized, one is able to practice.
Relying on what one has cultivated oneself, one is able to explain it to others;
this is precisely what the Sūtra refers to as the "penetration of the tenet" (siddhānta-praveśa) and the "penetration of the teaching" (deśanā-praveśa).
The penetration of the tenet constitutes spiritual practice.
The teaching is explained for the sake of the ignorant;
it is for the purpose of clarifying such meanings that this treatise was composed.
To elucidate its fundamental tenets:
There are two aspects to cultivation:
first, clarifying the fundamental tenet;
second, clarifying the ultimate goal.
There are two fundamental pillars:
first, the Mahāyāna teachings;
second, the Mahāyāna principles.
There are two goals:
first, the practice of the Mahāyāna;
second, the fruit of the Mahāyāna.
The Mahāyāna teachings refer to the doctrines such as those concerning the one mind and its two gates;
these expressive teachings are merely provisional designations, though they skillfully accord with the ultimate reality.
Because this is worthy of veneration.
The principle of the Mahāyāna refers to the dharma and its meaning.
What is called "Dharma" refers to the Dharma of the one mind and its two gates.
What is called "meaning" refers to—
This refers to the three great meanings of essence, characteristic, and function.
These phenomena and their meanings are the true objects of exposition and are entirely without falsehood;
they are worthy of veneration because they are sovereign.
A Mahāyāna practitioner is characterized by faith and practice.
Faith refers to the four kinds of faith.
"Practice" refers to the five practices,
for they are that toward which the practitioner proceeds.
As for the "fruit of the Mahāyāna":
This refers to the Great Dharma-body.
This Great Body of Dharma possesses its essential nature, characteristics, and functions;
it is that which was previously practiced as the cause and that toward which one has ultimately returned.
These various points will be explained below;
those who wish for a detailed exposition should seek them out from the citations.
This concludes the commentary on the treatise.
There are two parts to this exposition:
first, an explanation of the title;
second, a presentation of the treatise.
The explanation of the title has three parts:
first, explaining "Mahāyāna";
second, clarifying "Awakening of Faith."
Third, regarding the words of the commentary:
that which is called the Mahāyāna refers to the single mind.
As for the term "Great," it is established as a name based on its essential nature,
because it encompasses all things extensively.
What is called a "vehicle" (yāna) is established by way of metaphor;
it is so designated because it is capable of conveying [one] forward.
This means that this single mind can contain the meanings of the two gates, the three greatnesses, and so forth;
because it encompasses everything—ordinary and sage, defiled and pure—it is called "great.
By virtue of this, it is able to give rise to and sustain the myriad dharmas.
Because the causal conditions for the sublime destiny of all beings result in fruition, it is called a "vehicle" (*yāna*).
Consequently, based on this mind, the teaching, the principle, the practice, and the fruition— which constitute the expressed and the expresser—
are all termed the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the statement "arising faith" because it arises from the mind of the Mahāyāna:
"arising" (qi) means "to initiate.
This signifies that the Mahāyāna teaching is that which is capable of initiating faith.
It is characterized by a mind of patient acceptance and delight that is pure.
Because it is initiated through the Mahāyāna teachings and gives rise to the practice of faith toward the supreme principle and its fruit, it is called "Arousing Faith" (*qǐxìn*).
What is called "treatise" (śāstra) has the meaning of decisive determination.
It decisively distinguishes and analyzes the meanings of principle, practice, and fruition, thereby engendering understanding in others.
Therefore, it is called a "treatise" (śāstra). In brief,
it is a treatise that enables sentient beings to give rise to faith in this Mahāyāna.
It is titled the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* (Treatise on the Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna),
composed by the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa, as clarified in the extensive commentary on the "Gate of Illumination" (*Prasphuṭapadā*). Regarding the treatise:
"Homage to those who have reached the limit of the ten directions up to those who practice according to reality as it is.
[Commentary: The following is the second section, which explains the meaning of the treatise's text. This is divided into three parts.
The first three verses pay homage and state the purpose;
this constitutes the introductory section (*nidāna*).
From the words "The treatise says" (*śāstram āha*) onwards is the formal establishment of the body of the treatise.
This is the main body of the text.
The subsequent verse constitutes the conclusion, vow, and dedication for its circulation.
Within the prologue, there are two parts.
The first part reveals the homage;
the latter clarifies the intent of the composition.
This is the former.
Now, wishing to compose this treatise, I rely upon [the power of the Triple Gem] and request their grace.
Therefore, at the very beginning, I take refuge in the Three Jewels.
This is the second section of the text.
The two characters "take refuge" (*namas*) express the utmost sincerity of the one who takes refuge.
The passage beginning with "Throughout the ten directions" reveals the profundity and vastness of that which is taken refuge in.
As for what is meant by "taking refuge":
It has two meanings:
first, the meaning of respectful compliance;
second, the meaning of retribution and orientation.
"Life" has two meanings: first, the life of instruction;
second, the life of the body.
Desiring to lead sentient beings to cultivate the Buddha’s teachings so that they may accord with the source of their own fundamental mind, he composed this treatise.
Because he offers his body and life to take refuge in the Triple Gem and relies upon its power to request the bestowal of grace, it is said that he "takes refuge."
Within that which is taken as refuge, there are further two sections:
"pervading the ten directions" refers to the scope of those who are honored;
"supreme and so forth" refers to the qualities of the object of refuge itself.
Regarding "the Three Jewels worthy of veneration throughout the ten directions":
this does not mean venerating only the Three Jewels of a single direction.
One pays homage to all the Three Jewels existing in every single land throughout the ten directions.
The phrase "manifesting homage exhaustively" uses the expression "ten directions" to indicate its universal reach.
Within the Three Jewels, the first three phrases manifest the Jewel of the Buddha.
The term "supreme" (parama) indicates the Buddha,
because his three bodies (trikāya) transcend all others;
it is called "supreme" because it surpasses the inferior.
"Surpassing causes" is called "victory.
"Karma" refers to karmic function;
that is to say, the three wheels, the three virtues, and the two benefits of the Buddha-body’s karmic function.
The term "thorough knowledge" (parijñā) reveals the Buddha’s mental activity and the functional power of his great wisdom-virtue.
Because the mind possesses the light of great wisdom that shines everywhere and is capable of universal knowledge.
There are two kinds of universal knowledge:
first, true wisdom (*tattvajñāna*).
The conventional wisdom of the second type universally knows the gate of the *tathatā* (suchness) of the mind, including its qualities as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
it also universally knows the gate of the arising and ceasing of the mind, including the distinctions of its conditions.
Regarding these two gateways, one who possesses profound discernment, unerring and universal knowledge,
and unimpeded mastery [is so called] to manifest the great power and function of the Buddha’s bodily karma and meditative concentration.
Because one gives rise to an unimpeded and sovereign body of form based on meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
there are four kinds of non-obstruction:
first, non-obstruction between the large and the small.
Although each individual sense organ pervades the entire Dharma-realm,
they do not destroy the nature of the organs nor disparage the characteristics of the organs;
second, they function interchangeably without obstruction.
Although each individual faculty functions in mutual interaction with the others,
it neither loses its nature as a faculty nor abandons its characteristic marks; thus,
the three principles and phenomena are unimpeded.
Although form appears manifest, its essential nature is twofold;
although its wondrous substance is quiescent, its functional activity is boundless.
Its fourfold responsiveness to sentient beings is unimpeded.
Although the bodies manifested through multiple functions are indistinguishable as they appear universally,
and although the pervasive response of the perfect wisdom is total throughout its entire substance,
because of the Great Samādhi, form arises from the very source of reality itself.
Because its meaning does not depend on another, it is called "sovereign.
This refers entirely to the Buddha-jewel’s utilization for its own benefit.
Regarding the phrase "saving the world" and so forth:
This reveals the Buddha’s verbal karma,
which is the functional virtue of great compassion acting for the benefit of others.
It is through the virtue of great compassion that he is able to initiate verbal karma.
It is said that because it arises for the benefit of others through conditions consisting of the sublime Dharma,
"world" (*loka*) refers to sentient beings;
they are so called because they can be confronted and destroyed, and thus ought to be rescued.
Regarding the term "Great Compassion" (mahākaruṇā):
it is called "Great Compassion" because it manifests the Buddha’s capacity for salvation through its objective conditions;
that is to say, among the three types of compassion, it is the compassion without an object (nirālambana-karuṇā).
It is not like the compassion regarding self and dharmas held by ordinary beings and those of the Small Vehicle, which is neither constant nor universal.
As for the phrase "because of delivering all sentient beings," this means that the qualities of the provisional person are attributed to the individual.
One who possesses the aforementioned three wheels, three virtues, and two benefits is designated as such.
The following two phrases reveal the Jewel of the Dharma,
namely, the two greats of essence and characteristic within the three greatnesses.
Because it is subsumed by the great treasure of the Buddha’s activity.
As for the term "and so forth" (et cetera),
it carries two meanings.
First, the meaning of "contradiction," which indicates that this Jewel of the Dharma and the aforementioned Jewel of the Buddha are two distinct entities.
Second, the meaning of "containing the vehicle" (yāna).
It is not only that one reveres the preceding Great Jewel of the Buddha,
but also that one reveres the Jewel of the Dharma in its essential nature and characteristics;
for the sake of manifesting these two meanings, the word "and" (及) is employed.
Regarding the phrase "that body":
it refers to the three bodies of the Buddha, which receive that name in relation to this Dharma-jewel.
Regarding the phrase "essential nature and characteristics": [it refers to...]
"Essence" refers to the greatness of essence;
"characteristics" refers to the greatness of characteristics.
These are the essence and characteristics of the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) of the aforementioned great dharma-jewel.
Therefore, it is said to be the essential nature and characteristics of that body.
Among the four dharmas of teaching, principle, practice, and fruit,
this refers to the profound and perfect dharma of the revealed principle and fruit.
Therefore, by citing the Buddha, his Dharma is recorded.
This phrase specifically brings forth the essential nature and characteristics of the Jewel of the Dharma.
As for the term "dharma-nature" (dharmatā):
This reveals that this treasure of Dharma does not merely constitute the essence and characteristics of the preceding Buddhas,
but also constitutes the essential nature of all phenomena.
Because it is the nature of phenomena, it is called the "Dharmatā" (the nature of phenomena).
Regarding the term "True Suchness" (tathatā):
it reveals that although this Jewel of the Dharma serves as the essential nature of all phenomena,
it differs from those phenomena and is devoid of delusion.
Because it is entirely real and not false, it is called "true" (satya).
Because it is easy to reveal what is not real, it is called "suchness" (tathatā).
As for the term "ocean," it serves as a metaphor to illustrate two meanings.
First, the meaning is revealed by means of an analogy:
the Dharma Jewel, in accordance with conditions, produces all phenomena;
its nature is neither false nor real.
It is like the waters of the great ocean, which form waves due to the wind;
although the waves arise and cease,
the nature of moisture has no substantial reality.
One should know that the principle herein is likewise.
Second, by means of the analogy, the qualities are revealed;
these qualities reveal the Jewel of the Dharma.
Because they possess virtues as vast as the ocean,
it is said in the *Nityamegha-parivarta*:
"For example, the precious treasures within the deep great ocean are inexhaustible," and so forth.
...and so on, as explained at length.
Within the Jewel of the Sangha there are two phrases;
therein, the first phrase cites a person of virtuous qualities.
The Sangha encompasses both ordinary and noble beings, as well as those of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles.
Within this context, the noble Sangha of the Mahāyāna refers to Bodhisattvas on the stages (bhūmi);
by practicing even a single practice, all ten thousand practices are simultaneously perfected.
Each and every one of these practices is equal to the Dharma-realm and is obtained through the accumulation of merit.
For this reason, he is called a person of immeasurable merit.
Because he is able to encompass all virtues, he is named a "Treasury" (garbha).
The latter phrase clarifies the stage of practice upon which a person relies,
as explained below in the treatise:
the permeation by the power of the Dharma is the precursor to the stages (*bhūmi*).
Practicing according to reality is the practice of the stages (*bhūmi*).
Fulfilling the skillful means is the stage of fulfillment (*paripūrṇa*).
Here, by citing the practice of the stages, the stage of fulfillment is recorded concurrently.
Therefore, it is said: "practicing according to reality," and so forth. The Treatise states:
"It is because one desires to lead sentient beings to the point where the lineage of the Buddha remains uninterrupted. Commentary:
This is the statement of intent;
that is, it describes the purpose for composing this treatise in relation to the Triple Gem.
The text consists of four sentences.
This constitutes four meanings.
The first phrase clarifies the sentient beings for whose sake [the teaching is given].
Although sentient beings are numerous, they do not exceed three categories.
First, the group of those fixed in error (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*),
who have not yet given rise to faith for ten thousand kalpas;
second, the group of those who are not fixed (*aniyata-rāśi*).
Those whose faith is not yet fixed after ten thousand kalpas;
those of the three groups of the correctly determined;
and those in the stage of the ten abodes after ten thousand kalpas.
Now, as for the phrase "in order to cause sentient beings [to attain it]," this refers specifically to those in the intermediate indeterminate group,
so that their faith may become fixed.
It also encompasses sentient beings of both the heterodox and orthodox groups,
causing them to achieve faith and increase their understanding and practice;
this phrase reveals the obstacles that are eliminated.
There are two kinds of hindrances:
namely, doubt and attachment.
Because one is deluded by doubt regarding the truth, one loses the bliss of reality.
Because clinging gives rise to delusion, one plants the causes of suffering;
therefore, the subsequent sections of this treatise reveal the correct meaning to explain the fundamental principle, thereby enabling the realization of true bliss.
By counteracting false attachments, it eliminates the view of a personal self and causes one to abandon the causes of suffering.
Therefore, it is said that this removes doubt and abandons false attachments.
Next, the third phrase reveals the stage of the accomplished virtues,
so as to cause sentient beings to rely on the Mahāyāna teachings, contemplate the Mahāyāna principle, realize the Mahāyāna fruit, and give rise to the practice of right faith in the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the statement "arousing right faith in the Mahāyāna":

those who practice with right faith are precisely what the treatise below describes as the three types of generating the mind of enlightenment (cittotpāda), the four kinds of faith, and the five practices.
It is called "faith" because it overturns the aforementioned doubt;
it is called "right" because it overturns the aforementioned error.
The latter phrase reveals the stage into which one enters.
It is intended that they may enter the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotrabhūmi*) and certainly succeed to the fruit of Buddhahood;
that they may themselves rely on the Dharma so that the lineage of the Buddha-seed continues and they are able to teach it to others,
thereby ensuring the continuity of the Dharma.

It causes the Buddha-lineage of others to remain unbroken as well, because the three kinds of Buddha-nature—namely, that of oneself, of others, and of the True Teaching—are able to continue in succession.
Therefore, it is said: "Because the Buddha-lineage is not severed."
The Treatise says:
There is a dharma capable of arising; therefore, it should be explained. The Commentary says:
Next, the second section below clarifies the main body of the treatise (*śāstra*).
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the preliminary statement of the consent to explain;
second, the actual presentation of what is to be explained.
This is the first [point].
Regarding the phrase "the discourse says":
this distinguishes the discourse from other treatises (*śāstra*) and clarifies the teaching that functions as the expressive medium (*vyañjana*).
Regarding the phrase "there are dharmas,
etc.," this cites the dharmas that are expressed in order to demonstrate that there are objects of perception which bring benefit.
"Therefore, it should be explained" indicates the teaching that expresses [the meaning];
it means "it should be explained in accordance with the Dharma."
This means that since this expressed teaching possesses these expressed meanings— namely,
the dharmas of "one mind," "two gates," and "three greatnesses"— which can give rise to the faculty of faith in the Mahāyāna among sentient beings,
this expressive teaching must certainly be expounded.
One who has faith in the Mahāyāna believes in their own nature;
they know that the mind is falsely stirred and that there are no external objects prior to it.
This faith is definitively able to sustain and increase one's own and others' virtues;
therefore, it is called the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).
Treatise.
The exposition consists of five parts. The commentary states:
Next follows the second section, which formally presents what is to be explained;
this contains three sub-sections.
First, the number is raised to provide a general indication;
next, the names are listed according to that number;
finally, the characteristics are distinguished according to those names.
Next is the first [section].
The treatise asks:
"What are the five? up to the section on the benefits of exhortation to practice. The commentary states:
This is the enumeration of the names.
To say that they did not originate spontaneously but must have a source is what is meant by "causes and conditions" (hetu-pratyaya).
Because it takes up what remains outside the [preceding] sections, it is called the "Section on Divisions" (Vibhāga).
Since its purpose is to briefly indicate the essentials of the sūtra so as to inspire faith in sentient beings,
it is named the "Section on Establishing the Meaning" (Śāstrārthasanniveśa).
Since the essential points have already been summarized briefly,
it is now appropriate to provide a detailed exposition to bring about understanding;
this is called the Section on Exposition.
Based on this interpretation, understanding arises.
Next, it is appropriate to initiate practice;
because it causes practice to arise, it is called the "stage of faith in practice" (*pratipattisaddhāṅga*).
Although he manifests conduct that appears dull-witted and indolent,
he exerts effort to encourage others toward cultivation.
This is titled "The Section on Exhorting to Cultivate Beneficial Merit.

Treatise: First, the section on the causal conditions (*nidāna*). Commentary: * *Nidāna-bhāga-prathama-vyākhyānam*. (Exposition of the first part, the section on the causal conditions. * *Vyākhyānam āha*: (The commentary states: (Note: The provided text contains the title of the section and the opening phrase of the treatise/commentary. The term "述曰" (*shù yuē*) is a traditional Chinese formulaic marker meaning "the commentary says" or "it is stated," indicating the beginning of the explanatory portion following the title.)
The following third section distinguishes the characteristics based on their names;
it provides a detailed explanation of the fifth division,
which is itself divided into five parts.
The section on the initial causes and conditions is further divided into two parts:
first, the heading that states the name of the section;
second, the detailed exposition of its meaning.
This is the first [point].
The term "causal condition" (*nidāna*) carries the meaning of "reason," "purpose," and "initiation";
this is the meaning of "causal condition."
Treatise.
Question: Why did [the author] compose this treatise upon arriving? Commentary:
From here below is the second section, which specifically elucidates its meaning.
Among these, there are four questions and answers that are difficult to resolve;
this is the first statement.
Treatise:
The answer states: "These causal conditions are of eight kinds. The commentary states:
The following response has three parts;
first, the number is cited as a general answer.
Next, the meaning is distinguished according to number;
this is the first part, which concludes by answering the question posed.
Treatise:
What are the eight [reasons] up to "for the sake of gain and honor"? Commentary:
Next, the second section distinguishes the meaning according to number.
A separate analysis of eight causes is presented,
which is divided into eight parts;
among these, the first is the cause of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Subsequently, these seven types are specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) causes.
As for general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*),
there are three meanings.
First, it is composed by way of penetrating all treatises;
for it penetrates all treatises so that one may leave suffering behind and attain happiness.
Second, it is composed by way of penetrating all faculties.
The purpose served is not merely for the sake of those in the indeterminate group;
rather, it functions throughout all stages.
Furthermore, its initiation is not merely for the sake of establishing the formal thesis.
"All sufferings" refers to the eight sufferings,
the three sufferings, and the two sufferings of birth and death;
it means being free from all these general and specific sufferings.
Ultimate bliss refers to the bliss of unsurpassed bodhi and great nirvana;
for that which is attained by the two vehicles is not ultimate.

"Neither seeking these things" means that the author of the treatise intends to show that neither he himself nor sentient beings seek these things, yet he has composed this treatise. Thus says the treatise.
"Second, it is for the sake of reaching non-erroneousness. The commentary states:
"The seven types [of causes] following below are specific-characteristic causes;
they serve solely as the grounds for the composition of this treatise."
Therefore, it is revealed that what is intended is not to be applied universally,
but solely for the purpose of initiating the text concerning the seven locations.
As for what is called the fundamental meaning of the Tathāgata:
This single mind is precisely the fundamental and initial awakening (mūla-ādi-bodhi),
the root of the Tathāgata;
this fundamental awakening is termed "Suchness" (tathatā).
Initial awakening is called "coming";
because the initial and the fundamental are not different, it is called "Tathāgata.
For this reason, although sentient beings possess the true principle, they have not yet given rise to wisdom.
It illuminates suchness and yet does not come;
that is to say, because the Tathāgata is established in dependence upon the mind, this is explained as the fundamental meaning of the Tathāgata.
This meaning is demonstrated in the "Section on Establishing the Meaning" and in the "Explanation of the Correct Meaning."
It causes those sentient beings of the three stages of worthiness to accord with the wisdom of contemplation;
hence it is called "correct understanding.
This means that by counteracting false attachments and departing from the view of a personal self (*pudgala-ātman*), the wisdom of contemplation is free from inversion and is thus termed "unerring."
Treatise:
These three are for the purpose of causing one to reach the stage of non-retrogressive faith. Commentary:
The maturation of the roots of goodness refers to those who have reached the final mind of faith throughout the ten directions.
Because one has cultivated the ten roots of goodness to their own fulfillment,
it is called "maturation.
For such a person, I shall now explain the three types of resolve that constitute the characteristics of setting out upon the path within the section on interpretation.
This causes them to enter the stages from the first abode (*prathamā vihārā*) upward, so that they may abide in the Mahāyāna and become capable of practicing with non-retrogressive faith.
Treatise:
Fourth, it is for the purpose of causing them to reach the stage of cultivated faith (*śraddhā*). Commentary:
"Having meager roots of goodness" refers to those at the stage of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).
Because they have not yet fulfilled the cultivation of the virtues of the ten faiths,
it is said that their roots are "meager."
For their sake, he clearly expounds the four faiths and four practices of the initial stage of the section on cultivation,
causing them to practice them universally until they reach the stage of perfected faith;
therefore, it is said that "one cultivates the mind of faith."
Treatise:
Fifth, it is for the purpose of reaching and emerging from the net of heterodoxy. Commentary:
The initial stage of the ten levels of faith consists of three grades.
That is to say, there are the inferior, the middling,
and the superior. Because those of the inferior grade have committed much evil karma,
they encounter many obstacles despite lacking any spiritual practice.
For their sake, he clearly expounded the sections on the practice of prostrating to the Buddhas, repenting,
and so forth, causing them to cultivate these practices to eliminate their karmic obstacles and skillfully guiding their minds so that they would not commit further evil.
This gradually distances one from the causes of delusion, pride, and evil karma.
The Treatise states:
Sixth, it is for the purpose of demonstrating the faults of the minds of those who have reached the level of the Two Vehicles. The Commentary says:

Because those of middling capacity within the first mind of the ten stages of faith still possess the minds of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and followers of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*),
this constitutes a grave error regarding their progress toward the Mahāyāna. Therefore,
texts such as those on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are revealed for their sake.
This causes them to practice as an antidote.
Regarding the seventh point, it is for the purpose of demonstrating the ultimate regression of faith. The commentary states:
For those of superior capacity at the initial stage of the ten levels of faith,
who fear that they will not encounter a Buddha in this degenerate age and thus find it difficult to perfect their practice of faith— yet whose resolve never wavers—
for their sake, this text on being born in the Pure Land is clearly expounded.
Taking the mindfulness of all Buddhas as one's object,
one employs skillful means to ensure rebirth in their presence;
this is non-retrogressive faith.
Treatise:
Eighth, because it demonstrates the ultimate goal and exhorts one to practice. Commentary:
For those of the three grades who have first attained the initial mind of the ten faiths, they are prone to regression and difficult to advance as they first begin their practice.
For their sake, he clearly explains and encourages them to practice for the sake of benefit;
he points out their losses and gains to encourage them to cultivate relinquishment;
and he speaks of demonstrating benefits to encourage the practice of cultivation and so forth.
Treatise.
There are such causes and conditions for composing this treatise. Commentary:
The preceding section established the categories based on their enumeration to clarify the meaning.
This concludes the response to the question posed in the treatise.
Question: Why is it necessary to state this again? Commentary: [The reason is as follows.]

This is the third objection: namely, that all the propositions, categories, and meanings explained by the eight preceding reasons are fully contained within the various sūtras, and they all serve to enable sentient beings to abandon suffering and attain happiness.
Now, in composing this treatise, you restate those same doctrines;
is this not for the sake of seeking fame, profit, and the like?
For this reason, it is asked: "Why is it necessary to restate them?"
Treatise:
The answer states, "Up to the distinction of the conditions for liberation. Commentary:
From here below is the fourth section, which addresses the objections raised.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, a brief general response to the objections;
second, an extensive refutation of lingering doubts.
This concludes the exposition of this treatise;
it is the first [section].
Although this teaching exists within the Sūtras, [it is presented here for clarification].
He cites the opponent's question and allows their objection to stand;
then, from the words "Sentient beings... onwards, he answers that objection and removes their state of doubt.
Regarding the phrase "those whose faculties and practices are not equal":
This clarifies the similarities and differences among the faculties (*indriya*).

One is able to produce all sounds from a single sound without exception;
yet each individual sound pervades the entire Dharma-realm,
and the melodic tones remain forever without confusion.
If this sound were crooked and not pervasive,
it would be sound but not perfect;
if it were to become perfectly pervasive, it would lose its melodic quality.
Thus, it is perfect yet not mere sound;
yet now, it is universally pervasive without destroying its melodic curves,

It is by virtue of this principle that the perfect voice is achieved;

"Based on non-awakening, there is initial awakening. Treatise: From "the source of the mind of non-awakening" up to "not yet ultimate awakening. Commentary: [The text states: Based on non-awakening, there is initial awakening. Regarding this, the commentary says: from "the source of the mind of non-awakening" to "not yet ultimate awakening. This means that because one does not awaken to the source of the mind, there is non-awakening; based upon this non-awakening, there is the designation of initial awakening. Furthermore, because one has not yet fully awakened to the principle of the One Mind, it is called "not yet ultimate awakening. Thus, although there is the name of initial awakening, it is in fact non-awakening. Because there is non-awakening, there is initial awakening; because there is initial awakening, there is non-awakening. Therefore, it is said that based on non-awakening, there is initial awakening. This is the meaning. As for "from the source of the mind of non-awakening," this refers to the source of the mind of non-awakening. What is meant by "source"? It means the fundamental origin. It is like the source of a river; it is the place where all waters flow forth. Here, the source of the mind of non-awakening is likewise the fundamental origin from which all delusions arise. It is also called the "fundamental ignorance" (mūlāvidyā). This fundamental ignorance is precisely the source of the mind of non-awakening. Therefore, it is called "from the source of the mind of non-awakening. "To the extent of not yet being ultimate awakening" means that although one has attained initial awakening, one has not yet fully awakened to the principle of the One Mind. Therefore, it is called "not yet ultimate awakening. This is the meaning. Furthermore, "initial awakening" is a term established based on non-awakening; it is not a name established based on true awakening. Why? Because it is not yet ultimate awakening. If it were ultimate awakening, it would be called "ultimate awakening" and not "initial awakening. Therefore, it is known that initial awakening is a name established based on non-awakening. This is the meaning. Furthermore, "non-awakening" is the substance, while "initial awakening" is the function. Because there is the substance of non-awakening, there is the function of initial awakening. Therefore, it is said that based on non-awakening, there is initial awakening. This is the meaning. Furthermore, "non-awakening" is the cause, while "initial awakening" is the effect. Because there is the cause of non-awakening, there is the effect of initial awakening. Therefore, it is said that based on non-awakening, there is initial awakening. This is the meaning. Furthermore, "non-awakening" is the delusion, while "initial awakening" is the antidote. Because there is the delusion of non-awakening, there is the antidote of initial awakening. Therefore, it is said that based on non-awakening, there is initial awakening. This is the meaning. Furthermore, "non-awakening" is the darkness, while "initial awakening" is the light. Because there is the darkness of non-awakening, there is the light of initial awakening. Therefore, it is said that based on non-awakening, there is initial awakening. This is the meaning. Furthermore, "non-awakening" is the false, while "initial awakening" is the true. Because there is the falsity of non-awakening, there is the truth of initial awakening. Therefore, it is said that based on non-awakening, there is initial awakening. This is the meaning. Furthermore, "non-awakening" is the other-dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva), while "initial awakening" is the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva).

Regarding the four meanings of emptiness:
it is empty of all marks, it can contain all things, it is free from defilement and reveals purity, and it manifests all things.
Regarding the four meanings of the mirror:
The void is without external objects, yet its substance contains all forms; it is free from all defilements, and the manifestation of forms serves as their functional utility.
By means of this analogy of the empty mirror, the True [Suchness] is illustrated.
Treatise:
What are the four? They are for the purpose of the meaning of awakening and illumination.
Commentary: The following provides the detailed explanation.
The four meanings are explained individually,
divided into four sections;
this is the first.
"Mirror of reality as it is" (yathābhūta-śūnyatā-maṇḍala) is the designation of its name.
As for the term "reality as it is" (yathābhūta):
This is the true essence itself.
Because its true virtue is not void, it is called "as-it-is" (yathābhūta).
As for that which is called "emptiness":
It is named "delusion" in contrast to that which is not delusive.
Because the essence of original enlightenment is without delusion,
and because phenomena are empty and without delusion, it is called "emptiness as it truly is" (yathābhūta-śūnyatā).
Because it is free from delusion, its essence is luminous and pure,
like a clear mirror.
The following section explains this meaning in detail.
Because the inverted mind and delusory objects are fundamentally incompatible, it is said that one "remains far removed from the characteristics of mind and its objects.
Since this mind and these objects are fundamentally non-existent, they do not appear within awakening, just as a tortoise's hair does not appear in a mirror.
Therefore, it is said that there is no dharma that can be manifested.
Because nothing can be manifested, the delusive dharmas of mind and objects, when compared to original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), are not what is illuminated;
and original enlightenment, when compared to mind and objects, is not that which performs the illumination.
Since that which is illuminated does not exist,
and because the illuminator likewise does not exist,
it is said that this is not the meaning of cognitive illumination.
This demonstrates that there is no imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) which can manifest as a substantial reality, and therefore it is not an object of cognitive awareness.
The subsequent statement regarding "the object appearing therein" refers to this.
It is also not contradictory that the dependent nature appears as such.
The treatise states: "Second, because it perfumes the causes and reaches the sentient beings. The commentary says:
This is the second meaning.
"Caused by a mirror" indicates its name;
that which can produce the fruit of cognition is termed the "cause."
Because this can internally permeate [the mind], it is called "perfuming" (vāsanā);
because it can manifest all phenomena, it is termed a "mirror.
Below, its characteristics are further explained.
The text consists of three sections.

That which is called "truly not empty" (*yathābhūtam aśūnyam*) sets forth the essence of the cause; because it possesses the characteristics of untainted (*anāsrava*) qualities and virtues as its true essence, it is said to be "truly not empty."
Because it is not empty, it is able to serve as the direct cause for that initial awakening;
thus, "not empty" carries the meaning of being a cause.
The phrase "all things" and below explains the meaning of the mirror.
This means that all phenomena have no separate essence apart from this mind,
just as reflections appear within a mirror.
As for the statement "they do not go out":
The enlightened mind awaits perfuming to manifest all phenomena;
it does not spontaneously produce them without awaiting perfuming,
for the various phenomena that are manifested do not exist apart from the mind.
Regarding the statement "they do not enter":
it means that while the mind manifests all phenomena through transformation according to its habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*),
neither defiled nor pure phenomena enter from the outside.
Because the reflected images that appear do not defile the substance [of the mirror],
it is said that they are "not lost.
Although these various mirror-images do not emerge from within the reality or enter from without, [they are nonetheless present].
Yet it does not lose the dependent origination that is manifested;
for although the characteristics of objects are manifested, they do not lose their reality.
Thus it is said that it is "unimpaired."
Dharmas arise from the Truth;
because they do not differ from the nature of True Suchness and are identical with the Truth, they cannot be destroyed.
Although they appear and disappear according to conditions, they remain as such.
Because it is truly indestructible,
that which eternally abides in one mind is the realization of the identity of characteristics and essence.
All subsequent explanations are based on this same principle:

because the phenomena of dependent origination manifest within the mind without arising or ceasing, they have no separate substance; and because they have no separate substance, they are from the beginning equal and non-different from true suchness (*tathatā*).
Therefore, it is said that "the one mind is eternally abiding," and so forth.
Furthermore, the passage beginning with "Moreover, all" explains the meaning of perfuming (*vāsanā*):
because its nature is pure, it is able to manifest defiled phenomena.
Although it manifests, it cannot be defiled by defiled phenomena;
therefore, it is said that "it cannot be defiled by defiled phenomena.
This is because it was originally without defilement and is primordially pure.
Because the wisdom of original enlightenment has never moved,
it is said that the essence of wisdom is immovable.

Within this original enlightenment, not only is there no defilement, but because its virtuous qualities are not lacking even in the slightest, it is said to be "fully endowed with the untainted" (*anāsrava*).
This very quality of purity can permeate sentient beings, causing them to weary of birth and death and to joyfully seek nirvana;
therefore, it is said that it "permeates sentient beings.
Treatise.
Third, because the Dharma emerges as supremely pure and luminous. The commentary states:
This is the third [point]. Regarding "the Dharma emerging":
it refers to the emergence of the Dharma.
This indicates its name.
Because its essence and characteristics are non-empty, it is called "Dharma" (the Dharma).
Because it manifests from the two obstructions, it is termed "Emergence."
Because it destroys the characteristic of combination, it is called "separation.
Because it is pure, limpid, and bright, it is likened to a mirror.
Below this, the characteristics are analyzed.
Regarding the phrase "that which is not empty":
this explains the preceding term "dharma" (法) to reveal the essential nature of dharmas.
It refers to the dharma that is not empty due to the prior perfuming of causes.

Regarding the phrase "emerging from the hindrance of afflictions and the hindrance to knowledge," the character "emerge" (chū) is explained as manifesting the departure from entanglements (*paryavasthāna*),
because the pure *dharmakāya* emerges from this through the permanent severance of the two hindrances.
"Free from the characteristic of conjunction" explains the character "free" (li).
Because it has emerged from the two obstacles, there is no further conjunction of the characteristics of arising and ceasing consciousness.
"Pure and luminous" explains the character for "mirror":
it is called "pure" because it is free from manifold characteristics.
It is called "pure" because it emerges from obstruction and defilement;
it is called "luminous" because it is purely pure;
it is called a "mirror" because it is purely pure and luminous.
Treatise:
Fourth, because it manifests through the mindfulness reached by the perfuming of conditions. Commentary:
This is the fourth [point].
"The mirror of perfuming by conditions" is the designation of its name.
It is called "conditions" because it functions as a great external perfuming influence.
It is called "perfuming" (vāsanā) because it causes the arousal of wholesome states of mind;
it is likened to a mirror because it gives rise to the reflections of wholesome dharmas.
This means that when this aspect emerges from its entanglements, it acts as the wisdom of the mirror, capable of performing great functions and manifesting the myriad transformations.
Acting as conditions to stimulate the minds of sentient beings,
causing them to give rise to a sense of renunciation and joy and to initiate various preparatory practices, is called "conditioned perfuming.
These qualities of practice are reflections of the Buddha's wisdom.
Because it is never separate from the Buddha-wisdom, it is called a "mirror.
Thus, the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states:
"The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom can give rise to the reflections of all the wholesome dharmas of sentient beings."
In the section defining the characteristics below, there are two parts.
Regarding "those who depart in reliance upon the Dharma," this refers to the emergence of the causal conditions from the substance of perfuming.
The passage beginning with "Having universally illumined" reveals the characteristics of the conditions for perfuming.
This means that, based on the aforementioned Dharmakāya which has emerged from entanglements and is free from the characteristics of combination,
because it is pure, clear, and luminous, great wisdom arises.
Because the function of the meaning of light is to universally illumine the various mental states of sentient beings throughout the dharma-realm,
it manifests ten thousand transformations according to their thoughts and inclinations due to this universal illumination, thereby causing them to practice.
It is said that they cause [beings] to cultivate roots of goodness because these are in accordance with their respective portions of roots of goodness;
it is said that they manifest [these] because they appear in accordance with mindfulness. Thus says the Treatise.
Regarding the statement "from non-awakening to not being separate from fundamental awakening," the commentary states:
The meaning of awakening has already been explained;
below, non-awakening is revealed.
Within this, there are three parts: first, the explanation of fundamental non-awakening;
second, the manifestation of derivative non-awakening;
and third, the conclusion that returns the derivative to the fundamental.
Within the former, there are again two parts:
first, delusion is established based on awakening;
second, awakening is revealed based on delusion.
The beginning and middle [of this section] also consist of three parts:
namely, the Dharma, the analogy, and the synthesis.
This is the first, the Dharma.
This refers to those who do not know that the *dharmatā-tathatā* is one, yet still possess such thoughts.
This demonstrates that non-awakening exists in dependence upon awakening.
That thought has no intrinsic nature and is not separate from original awakening.
This reveals that there is no lack of illumination distinct from fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*).
Within the preceding [section], there are three meanings, namely:
"not knowing in accordance with reality."
This refers precisely to the deluding ignorance (*avidyā*).
For instance, it is said that "to accord with reality" means "the true reality.
As for the single dharma of *tathatā* (suchness):
This refers precisely to the phenomena that are objects of delusion.
The true essence is of a single flavor and is called "one" because it is free from thought;
yet, there are those who possess such thoughts.
This refers precisely to the eight consciousnesses of the mind, which are constituted by delusion.
That is to say, the true single flavor is the capacity for delusion;
ignorance (avidyā) is the failure to know in accordance with reality.
Because one perceives the conceptualizations of the eight consciousnesses, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
However, this ignorance has no substance apart from the Truth;
therefore, it is said that these conceptualizations lack intrinsic characteristics and are not separate from original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*).
Treatise:
It is just as when a person who is lost ceases to be lost upon reaching [their destination].
Commentary: This is an illustration.
The meaning is easy to understand. Regarding the treatise:
"Sentient beings are also like this; wherever they go, there is nothing they do not perceive. The commentary states:
This is the correspondence of these dharmas.
Original awakening (mūla-awakening), the true nature, is like the square location;
fundamental non-awakening (mūla-non-awakening) is like that which can cause delusion.
The movement of thoughts within mental karma is like "false direction.

Just as there is no separate "false west" apart from the "correct east," it is said that if one were to depart from the nature of awakening (*bodhi*), there would be no such thing as non-awakening (*abodhi*).
However, although this non-awakening and the aforementioned original awakening are neither identical nor different,
they do not depart from the nature of awakening; yet, despite not departing from awakening, [non-awakening] remains distinct.
"It is not identical to the nature of awakening.
Treatise:
"Because there is non-awakening, it can be described according to its own characteristics. Commentary: [As stated above.]
This refers to the manifestation of awakening based upon delusion.

Because there exists the mind of unreal appearances arising from non-awakening (*abodha*), one is able to know names and meanings; it is for this reason that true awakening is taught. This clarifies the essential function of the pure arising from within the unreal.
Because one is able to know names and meanings through false appearances,
the name "true awakening" is provisionally applied to these false appearances;
this is because, in its true essence, there are no names or appearances.
If one were to leave behind the mind of non-awakening and the self-characteristic of true awakening could be named,
this would clarify the principle that the real depends upon the delusive.
If one leaves behind non-awakening, there is no means by which the real can be explained.
Since that which is depended upon does not exist,
that which depends [upon it] does not exist;
therefore, both the dependent and the dependence are quiescent.

Next, the following clarifies the secondary and derivative lack of awakening (*abodha*), which is twofold:
first, it clarifies the subtle aspect;
second, it reveals the coarse aspect.
The beginning and the middle also each have two parts:
a general heading and a detailed explanation.
This is the first [of those].
The three subtleties constitute the characteristics,
while ignorance constitutes the essence;
because the essence and characteristics of the root and its branches are not separate from one another, they are called "associated."
This does not refer to the meaning associated with the King (the ālayavijñāna),
because these three subtle states are all defiled minds dissociated from the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
They constitute deluded mind based upon ignorance (*avidyā*).
Furthermore, ignorance arises based on the deluded mind;
therefore, it is called "associated and inseparable.
Treatise.
"What are the three? Up to 'because they do not depart from their causes. Commentary:
What follows below provides a detailed explanation.
This is the detailed explanation of the three subtle [defilements].
It is divided into three parts;
this is the first.
Regarding the "characteristic of the activity of ignorance":
This indicates its name.
It means that because the mind moves due to ignorance, it is called "karma";
thus, it is named the "phase of karma characterized by ignorance."
It does not mean that ignorance itself is called the "phase of karma.
Regarding the phrase "based on non-awakening," this explains that the ignorance mentioned in the heading refers to fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*).
"The movement of the mind is called karma" explains the character "karma" (業) mentioned in the heading.
Karma has two meanings.
It has the meaning of a single movement;
therefore it is said: "Because of non-awakening, the mind moves, and this is designated as karma.
Awakening is itself non-movement."
Returning to the original point to explain and establish the conclusion:
since there is no stirring of thought at the time of initial awakening,
we know that the present movement arises solely from non-awakening.
Because the second serves as the cause, it is said that "movement results in suffering.
When one attains the state of tranquility and non-conceptualization, this is precisely the wondrous fruit of Nirvana.
Thus, we know that present movement entails the afflictions of birth and death.
If the fruit does not depart from its cause,
then since the unmoving is pleasure,
the moving must necessarily be suffering.
Since there is no distinct time between the movement of causes and the arising of suffering effects,
it is said that they are "not separate.
Although this involves mental movement, it is extremely subtle.
The single characteristic of dependent origination, in which subject and object are undifferentiated,
corresponds precisely to the self-substance portion (*svabhāva-bhāga*) of the ālayavijñāna.
Treatise.
Second, that which is capable of seeing reaches the point where there is no seeing. The commentary states:
"The characteristic of being capable of seeing" is the designation of its name.

This statement regarding "being able to see" refers to the subsequent transformation of the dependent aspect, whereby it evolves from the preceding karmic consciousness to become the faculty of seeing. Therefore,
it is said that "because of the movement of the basis, one is able to see."
If it were by way of an inherently pure gate, there would be no capacity for seeing;
therefore, it is said that "if there is no movement, there is no seeing.
This conversely reveals that the capacity to see must necessarily depend on the principle of movement.
Although such a transformed aspect possesses the capacity for objective apprehension, it has not yet grasped the object;
because it is subtle, it is precisely the mind of the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*).
— Treatise.
Third, when the characteristics of objects reach one another, there are no objects. The commentary states:
"The characteristics of objects" is a designation of their names.
This refers to the "objective realm" (*viṣaya*).
It is because the evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) down to the manifesting consciousness (*nirmana-vijñāna*) can here manifest the appearances of the objective realm;
that is, by depending on the preceding aspect of evolution, it is able to manifest the objective realm.

It is said that because there is the capacity to see, objects appear falsely; if there were no conceptualization, then there would be no objects. Therefore, it is said that "if one is free from seeing, then there are no objects.
This conversely demonstrates that objects must necessarily depend upon the capacity to see.
This is precisely the mind that constitutes the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*).
These three preceding aspects are all activated by the power of fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*),
whereby the originally quiescent mind becomes this *ālaya-vijñāna* that is dissociated from wisdom.
Treatise:
Because there are objective spheres, six kinds of characteristics arise. Commentary:
The above clarifies the subtle characteristics.
The following section reveals the coarse characteristics.
Within it, there are two parts:
a general indication and a detailed explanation.
This is the heading.
The six characteristics all arise from the discriminative consciousness (vikalpa-vijñāna) based upon objective conditions.
Among these, the first two are of inferior grade,
as they consist of attachments arising based on their objects;
this is because all subtle afflictions are abandoned at the stages of the Path of Seeing and above.
The next two kinds arise from clinging and give rise to afflictions; these are of medium strength because they are severed by the followers of the Two Vehicles.
The final two kinds rely on karma to undergo retribution.
Because ordinary persons recognize the coarse afflictions of the superior grade,
the Sūtra says:
Stirred by the winds of objective spheres, the various waves of consciousness surge and arise.
The treatise asks:
"What are the six? up to "because of the pleasant and the unpleasant. The commentary states:
Next follows the detailed explanation.
The detailed explanation of the six coarse factors is divided into six parts.
This is the first [point].
It means that as long as one has not yet eliminated ignorance and lacks clear understanding,
one does not realize that the objective appearances manifested by the manifesting consciousness are all one's own mind and possess no inherent nature.
The initial arising of the conceptualization of defilement and purity within the categories of evil is called "conceptualizing defilement and the unlovely.
Treatise.
Second, because it continues in a succession until it reaches association without interruption. The commentary states:
Based on the previous analysis of pleasant and unpleasant objects, suffering and pleasure arise;
because the mind of perception and recollection is constantly continuous, it is called the characteristic of continuity (*saṃtati-lakṣaṇa*).

That is to say, based on the preceding moment of conceptualization, one gives rise to a pleasant feeling of craving toward an agreeable object and a painful feeling of craving toward a disagreeable object;
these thoughts arise repeatedly, forming a continuous succession that manifests before one.
And it is constantly associated and uninterrupted.
The Treatise says:
"Third, the characteristic of grasping, because attachment arises in the mind. The Commentary states:
Failing to realize that the previously grasped objects, such as suffering and pleasure, are empty and non-existent,
one gives rise to deep attachment;
this is called the characteristic of grasping.

This means that regarding the objects of suffering and pleasure previously recollected within that same mental continuum, one further develops deep attachment, maintains them, and does not relinquish them;
therefore, it is said that "the mind gives rise to attachment," and so forth.
(Treatise)
Fourth, because one calculates names up to the characteristics of named expressions. The commentary states:

Based upon the previously mentioned objects grasped through inversion, one further establishes names and expressions, thereby giving rise to conceptual discrimination and calculating the characteristics of names.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Names and characteristics constantly follow one another, giving rise to all delusive appearances.
Thus it is said that they depend upon false attachment and discrimination to establish provisional names and so forth.
[Treatise]
Fifth, the characteristic of initiating karma, up to various types of karma. The commentary states:
Based on the aforementioned conceptualization and the mind of attachment, one gives rise to afflictions such as greed;
these then impel the body and speech to create various types of karma.
This is able to summon the bitter fruits of the five destinies in the future;
this, then, is how afflictions and karma serve as the proximate causes of suffering.
Treatise.
Sixth, because the bonds of karma lead to a lack of sovereignty. The commentary states:
Once the causes of karma have been established, one undergoes the fruits in dependence upon that karma.
Cycling through the various realms of existence within the long wheel of birth and death,
one is bound by karma and lacks autonomy;
this is called the suffering of karmic bondage.
Therefore, it is said that one experiences the fruits of karma without mastery, and so forth.
The Treatise states:
"It should be understood that ignorance extends to the characteristic of non-awakening. The Commentary says:
The preceding section extensively elucidated the non-awakening of the branches and their offshoots;

"What are the two? As for 'the two,' it refers to their differing characteristics. Commentary:

That defilement and purity are both identical to the Truth is called "sameness" (tong).
The name and the characteristic can express the same meaning.
That the essence of defilement and purity is distinct is called "difference" (viśeṣa).
That difference possesses various specific forms is called "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa).
Why is this so? Because phenomena differ when their substance follows conditions,
yet they are identical when conditions are subsumed back into the substance.
Because conditions share the same essence, True Suchness is of a single flavor;
because the essence differs according to conditions, the two categories of ordinary beings and sages are distinguished.
Because of this distinction between ordinary beings and sages, the meaning of conventional truth is established.
Because True Suchness (tathatā) is singular, the principle of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) exists.
Such is the identity and difference between awakening and non-awakening.

Specifically, there is an objection that states:

Therefore, the commentary explains:

Within this, five aspects of consciousness are briefly revealed.
That which arises through non-awakening is,
first, the essential substance of the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*).
Because the entire body is moved by being perfumed,
that which is said to "see" is the transformation of the second consciousness.
Because the passive mind becomes capable of seeing,
that which is said to "manifest" refers to the third consciousness, the manifesting-consciousness (ālayavijñāna), which is the seeing-mind.
Furthermore, because it can manifest various objects,
that which is able to apprehend objects is the fourth consciousness, the *manovijñāna*.
Because it can grasp the objects manifested by the manifesting consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*),
that which gives rise to a continuous stream of mentation is the fifth, the *saṃtati-vijñāna*.
Because attachment toward objects arises and is not severed,
these five meanings successively transform one another;
based upon these meanings, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises.
Therefore, these five are called "mind" (manas),
whereas that mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is not their support;
thus, it is simply called "consciousness" (vijñāna).
Therefore, it is not called "manas.

Third, it is called "arrival" because it is always present before [the object]. Commentary:

This refers to the combination of the principle (dharma),
the illustration (dṛṣṭānta), and their synthesis. Specifically, "that which can manifest all objects" is the statement of the principle.

Based on the preceding aspect of the evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) that is capable of seeing, this manifesting consciousness (*nirbhāsa-vijñāna*) gives rise to the function of manifestation, presenting all objects.
That is to say, because the substance of this mind combines with ignorance (*avidyā*), through the power of perfuming (*vāsanā*), it manifests various and boundless realms.
It is able to manifest all objects because it is capable of doing so;
the phrase "just as a bright mirror manifests forms and images" is an illustration.
Just as a mirror manifests various images due to external objects,
the mind manifests various objects due to the uneven perfuming of ignorance.
The following illustrates the application of this principle.
Regarding the statement that the five sense objects appear simultaneously as they encounter their respective conditions without sequence:
this precisely corresponds to the preceding analogy.
That is to say, when the mind—consisting of karma and afflictions—is confronted by the perfuming of those very afflictions and karma, the five sense objects then manifest.
It does not arise sequentially in dependence upon mental attention (*manasikāra*).
In reality, this consciousness manifests all objects;
however, the term "only" (*kevala*) here refers specifically to its manifestation of the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).
Furthermore, taking the coarse and manifest as an illustration to conform with the analogy of colors appearing in a mirror,
the phrase "arising spontaneously at all times" is used to distinguish it from the six consciousnesses.
The six consciousnesses are frequently interrupted and do not manifest;
because they do not arise spontaneously at all times,
the phrase "always present" serves to distinguish them from the manas.
The manas is not the fundamental source of the various consciousnesses,
because it does not always arise prior to them.

Treatise.
"Abiding in the past until one is unaware of deluded thoughts. The commentary states:
The following section reveals the functional capacity.
The text consists of two parts.
First, it reveals the functions of the three preceding fundamental consciousnesses;
because the ālayavijñāna manifests through the transformation of karma,
it stores and conceals the seeds of all phenomena, both wholesome and unwholesome.
It is able to maintain the karmic seeds of wholesome and unwholesome actions performed in past lives,
ensuring they are not lost;
this clarifies that the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) is capable of sustaining these seeds.
Because it gathers the seeds of karma so that they are not lost,
and because good and evil fruits arise according to good and evil seeds,
it can bring to maturity the retributions of suffering and pleasure in the present and future without error.
This clarifies that the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is capable of giving rise to active manifestations (*pravṛtti*).
Thus, the fact that the causes and effects of the three periods of time do not lose their efficacy is due to the fundamental consciousness;
for this reason, it is said to be the functional capacity of the fundamental consciousness.
It can cause the two functions of consciousness—the subsequent manifestation of past events and the present—to become active.
Because that event-consciousness involves the conceptualization of dharma-grasping, it is able to reflect upon and contemplate matters of the three periods of time.

Therefore, it is said that they do not perceive false conceptualizations and the like. Treatise: "Thus, from the three periods of time up to the objects of the six sense-fields. Commentary: The commentary states: [This refers to the preceding discussion on the non-perception of deluded thoughts. Regarding the phrase "from the three periods of time up to the objects of the six sense-fields": this indicates that the various dharmas, whether past, present, or future, as well as the objective spheres of the six consciousnesses, are all devoid of intrinsic nature and are ultimately ungraspable. Thus, because one does not perceive these phenomena, one transcends the boundaries of conditioned existence. This is the meaning of the passage.
The above has extensively elucidated the characteristics of the transformation of the mind.
Next, the following section concludes by clarifying the meaning of depending upon the mind.

subsequently, doubts were resolved and the matter was extensively analyzed.
This is the first [section].
The text consists of two sections.
The passage "The three realms are false and illusory;
they are mind-only" is a sequential conclusion regarding the three realms.
Regarding the phrase "for this reason":
it is because the aforementioned single mind, following the activity of ignorance, gives rise to the five types of mental intention;
and the five types of consciousness and so forth are established in dependence upon that mind.
These five types of mentation collectively encompass the three realms; therefore,
it is said that the three realms arise solely through the transformation of the single mind,
and this mind evolves according to its habitual perfuming.
Marks that have substance but lack names are "empty";
those that lack substance yet appear to have it are "false.
Although these empty and false marks are of many kinds, [they are all alike].
However, upon investigating its cause, it is seen to be produced solely by the mind.
Thus it is said: "O Son of the Buddha, the triple world is mind-only.
The following section, beginning with "Apart from the mind," serves as a concluding summary by way of negation.
If the six sense objects were separated from that manifesting consciousness, the six sense objects would not exist.
By this reverse verification, one sees that the six sense objects are nothing but the One Mind;
therefore, it is said that apart from the mind, there are no six sense objects.

that presently existing objective realms can be perceived as distinct from the mind.

Furthermore, there may be doubt, saying:

Therefore, the latter two lines resolve this doubt by stating that the teaching of "seeing one's own mind" is intended to prevent the attachment to external objects;
in reality, it is not a case of the mind seeing the mind.
Just as a finger cannot cut itself with a blade,
how could there be seeing when the mind does not arise?
This is because the fundamental true mind is devoid of the characteristic of seeing.

Because the manifestation of great compassion is vast. Treatise: Cultivating the various pāramitās to gather and transform sentient beings. Commentary: The manifestation of great compassion is vast because it encompasses all sentient beings. Regarding the statement "cultivating the various pāramitās to gather and transform sentient beings," the meaning is as follows: by practicing the six perfections, one gathers in sentient beings through the four means of attraction (saṃgrahavastu) and causes them to enter the Mahāyāna path. This is called the cultivation of the pāramitās for the sake of gathering and transforming sentient beings. Furthermore, this cultivation of the pāramitās is not merely for the sake of one’s own benefit; rather, it is primarily for the purpose of benefiting others. Therefore, it is said that the manifestation of great compassion is vast. It is because of this vastness that the Bodhisattva practices the pāramitās to gather and transform all sentient beings. Thus, the cultivation of the pāramitās is the very function of great compassion. This is what is meant by "the manifestation of great compassion is vast. As for the phrase "cultivating the various pāramitās to gather and transform sentient beings," it refers to the fact that when a Bodhisattva practices the six perfections, they employ the four means of attraction—generosity, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and common purpose—to lead sentient beings to maturity and cause them to enter the Mahāyāna. This is the meaning of "gathering and transforming. Consequently, the cultivation of the pāramitās is established as the primary activity for the gathering and transformation of sentient beings. This concludes the commentary on the section concerning the cultivation of the pāramitās for the sake of gathering and transforming sentient beings.
This is the establishment of practice based on compassion.
One cultivates the various pāramitās,
thereby manifesting the conduct of the six perfections.
To gather and transform sentient beings,
one clarifies the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*);

Thus, benefiting others is itself one's own benefit;

This clarifies that there is no activity characterized by marks.
Furthermore, there is also no subsequent activity that can be employed;
this indicates the absence of marks.
As for the question "Why is this so?",
it challenges the meaning of signlessness (*animitta*).
The Buddha possesses the three bodies (*trikāya*) and manifests all signs (*nimitta*).
How can it be said that there is no aspect of function?
The meaning of the following answer is:
if one were to discard the responsive resonance between stimulus and response.
The Tathāgata is solely the wondrous principle, the fundamental wisdom, and the most supreme ultimate reality;
there are no further characteristics such as transformation, birth, or extinction,
but only the functioning that accords with conditions.
Function is itself non-function;
function is itself non-function.
It is like water being identical to waves.
Because they are immediately and eternally quiescent, it is said:
"The Buddhas are solely the Dharma-body, free from all conditioned activities."
Although the wondrous wisdom of ultimate truth is originally and eternally serene,
it responds to the perceptions of sentient beings with boundless utility;
thus, its constant function arises from within stillness.
Therefore it is said: "It is merely according to the benefit gained by sentient beings that [the Buddha] is described as having 'function' and so forth.

Next, the specific exposition follows.

this is the first.

The following explanation has two parts;
first, the actual manifestation of their functional characteristics.
The subsequent section consists of questions and answers that resolve doubts.
Within the preceding [section], there are also two parts.
The first directly reveals the characteristics of its function.
The subsequent detailed analysis is divided into two parts.
Within the first part, there are again two sections;
the first clarifies the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body).
This refers first to the subsequent *saṃbhogakāya*.
Those ordinary beings and followers of the two vehicles who perceive the Buddha through the conceptualization arising from their own minds [perceive it in this way].
This is seen based on the discriminative consciousness of phenomena (*vastu-vijñapti*).
This consciousness does not know that all objects are merely mind;
it clings to the existence of external objects.
Ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles have not yet transcended this consciousness when they perceive the Buddha-body;
relying on this coarse consciousness,
they differentiate the Buddha-body and see only the marks of the coarse physical form of the *nirmāṇakāya*.
Because they do not see the subtle and wondrous physical marks of the *saṃbhogakāya*,
that which is seen by those with small minds due to their wind-like [instability] is called the *nirmāṇakāya*. This is because,
through ignorance, they perceive what is coarse as being explained below.

Therefore, all the manifestations of the Buddha's marks that are perceived are appearances produced by the transformation of the *ālaya-vijñāna*. This is because, through the power of habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*),
the *pravṛtti-vijñāna*— driven by weariness with suffering and aspiration for cessation—
arouses the desire and prayer to behold the Buddha.
Thus, based on the manifest consciousness within the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), the pure and superior realm of the Buddha’s body appears.
This person does not know that the Buddha is manifested by the evolving consciousness;
they claim instead that the Buddha comes from outside, from the Tuṣita Heaven.
Failing to realize that form is, in its entirety, mind and thus lacks any spatial boundaries,
they cling to the notion that form exists apart from mind, thereby grasping at the Buddha’s body as having limited dimensions—
merely sixteen feet of physical appearance.
Because one cannot know form that has no limits as being without limits,
it is therefore called "not knowing exhaustively.
Treatise.
Second, that which relies on the ultimate is called the *saṃbhogakāya*. The commentary states:
The following clarifies the *saṃbhogakāya*, which contains three parts.
First, by means of consciousness, the person is raised to clarify what they perceive;
next, the characteristics of the two types of retribution based on the mind are correctly revealed.
The subsequent section clarifies the names by explaining their causes and effects;
this is the first [of those].
Bodhisattvas of the ten stages and above, relying upon the karmic consciousness (*karmavijñāna*), give rise to the wisdom of the perceiving subject.
It is by relying on this wisdom that one perceives the Buddha’s reward body (sambhogakāya);
therefore, it is said that one perceives by relying on the karmic consciousness (karmavijñāna).
This does not mean that the karmic consciousness itself is the perceiver.

Because this consciousness is subtle and cannot yet be perceived. Treatise: "The body possesses immeasurable colors up to immeasurable secondary marks. Commentary: Regarding the phrase "immeasurable colors," it means that from the time one first attains the stage of a Bodhisattva until the attainment of Buddhahood, the physical form produced by the transformation of the mind manifests various colors, such as blue, yellow, red, white, and so forth; hence it is called "immeasurable colors. Regarding "immeasurable marks," it means that from the time one first attains the stage of a Bodhisattva until the attainment of Buddhahood, the physical form produced by the transformation of the mind manifests various primary marks, such as the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor marks; hence it is called "immeasurable marks. Regarding "immeasurable secondary marks," it means that from the time one first attains the stage of a Bodhisattva until the attainment of Buddhahood, the physical form produced by the transformation of the mind manifests various secondary marks, such as the skin being soft and smooth, the hair growing from each pore, and so forth; hence it is called "immeasurable secondary marks. Furthermore, regarding the term "immeasurable," it refers to the fact that these three types of marks—colors, marks, and secondary marks—are each infinite in number, and thus they are collectively termed "immeasurable. This is what is meant by saying that the body possesses immeasurable colors, marks, and secondary marks.
