it is because it is equally and universally present within the minds of all sentient beings.
Because there is no volitional attention (*manasikāra*),
it is said to be "spontaneous" (*svarasa*);
this is because it can function without effort (*anābhoga*).
"Appearing solely in accordance with the minds of sentient beings" means that,

depending on their aversion or seeking, and according to their respective degrees of superiority or inferiority, the retributive and transformational [bodies] manifest through coarse or subtle functions.
"The minds of sentient beings are like a mirror and so forth" means:
Next is the presentation of the analogy.
From "In this way" onwards is the subsequent application to the dharma.
"The mind has impurities" refers to...
This means that those who are attached to the faults and afflictions of saṃsāra and lack the capacity to seek and behold the Buddha are said to be "defiled.
As for the non-manifestation of the dharmakāya:
although the dharmakāya pervades the minds of all sentient beings, it cannot manifest its retributive and transformational functions [for them].
It is not because of the defilements of afflictions that [the Buddha] does not appear;
for even in the minds of those such as Sunakṣatra, who are possessed of afflictions, the Buddha is seen.
Treatise.
The section on interpretation has already been explained; next, the section on practicing with faith will be discussed. The commentary states:
Next, the fourth section, "Practicing with Faith," is clarified.
Within this, there are two parts.
The first section concludes the preceding [material] and initiates the subsequent;
the latter correctly elucidates the practice of the faith of cultivation.
This is the first [part].
The preceding section has clarified the Mahāyāna through the "Explanatory Division.
Now, in order to clarify the *Arousing of Faith*, the "Cultivation of Faith" must be explained next.
[Treatise:]
Regarding this, based on those who have not yet entered [the path] up to those practicing with faith, the commentary states:
what follows below clearly elucidates this;
therein are three parts.
First, the intention is indicated by means of others;
second, it is extensively analyzed in relation to the Dharma;
and third, the expedient means for guarding against regression are provided.
This is the first point.
As for those sentient beings who have not yet entered right concentration,
they are also persons of the indeterminate group within the Mahāyāna.
However, within the indeterminate group (aniyata-rāśi), there are those who are superior and those who are inferior;
the superior advance,
while the inferior may regress.

The preceding section on the accomplishment of faith described the characteristics of generating the resolve for enlightenment for those superior persons whose faith is perfected, so as to cause them to generate the three minds and abide in the stage of correct determination.
This present section on the practice of faith is for those inferior persons who are subject to regression.
As in the previous case of the stage of "Abiding in the Resolve" (Prathamacittotpādavihāra),
although the specific aims differ, the destination is the same.
Treatise:
"What is the mind? How is it practiced? [The commentary] states:
Next follows the second section, which provides a detailed analysis by way of phenomena (*dharma*).
Within this, there are two parts.
Two questions were first posed,
and two answers were subsequently given;
this is the first [of the pair].
Treatise:
Briefly stated, there are four kinds of faith. Commentary:
The following response consists of two parts.
First, faith is answered;
subsequently, practice is clarified.
Within this, there are two parts.
First the heading;
later the explanation.
This is the first.
Treatise:
What are the four? Up to "for the sake of the dharma of suchness. Commentary:
The following explains the four kinds of faith.
This is divided into four parts.
This first [section] concerns the faith that possesses the cause for attaining Buddhahood.
Since True Suchness (tathatā) is the teacher of all Buddhas, [it is the object of this faith].
Because it is the source of all practices, it is called the "root.
Because one delights in mindful observation, it is termed "faith" (*śraddhā*).
Since it is the root of the three subsequent types of faith, it is elucidated first.
Treatise:
Second, faith in the Buddha because he has attained all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*).
Commentary: This faith is the fruit obtained through its causes.
Because the fruit and cause are established, they are explained next.
Treatise:
Third, faith in the dharmas up to the pāramitās. Commentary says:
This is precisely the faith that there is the practice for attaining Buddhahood;
since the Buddha is established by relying on the Dharma, it is explained next.
Among the four dharmas of teaching, principle, practice, and fruit:
The preceding section clarified the fruit of principle; this [section] concerns faith and practice.
Since faith necessarily arises from the teaching before one can believe in these three, faith in the teaching is also manifested herein.
Treatise:
Fourth is faith in the Sangha because they practice according to the ultimate truth. Commentary:
This refers to faith that there are persons who initiate and carry out spiritual practice.
Because the person from the Dharma-realm (the Indian master) propagated it, it is explained next.
Treatise:
There are five gates of practice that can accomplish this faith. Commentary says:
The following is the answer concerning the practice of cultivation.
This section contains three parts;
first, the enumeration of the items and the indication of their purpose.
Next, the names are listed according to their numerical order;
subsequently, they will be explained individually according to those names.
This is the first [section].

Although one previously studied and gave rise to the four kinds of non-virtuous faith, if these are not established through practice, that faith will not be firm; such unfirm faith will inevitably regress when encountering adverse conditions.
Therefore, one cultivates the five practices in order to perfect the four kinds of faith.
Treatise:
What are the five? From "What are the five" up to "the fifth is the gate of śamatha-vipaśyanā. Commentary:
This is a listing of names according to their number.
Because the meditative concentration and wisdom of all bodhisattvas transform through the simultaneous cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā,
and because these two are inseparable, the two pāramitās are combined as the fifth gate.
Treatise.
"How does one practice so as to advance toward bodhi? The commentary states:
Next follows the second type of gate, which provides a detailed explanation.
This consists of two parts.
First, the preceding four [points] are briefly clarified;
subsequently, *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are explained in detail.
Within the former, there are again two parts.
First, the four practices are explained individually;
subsequently, the profound obstacles are explained collectively.
Within the individual explanation, their four types of cultivation are revealed.
This is divided into four parts;
this is the first.
In the text, the initial section specifically clarifies the characteristics of the three kinds of giving as the primary causes for cultivation.
The following section provides a general exhortation regarding what should be cultivated:
one should abandon biased attachments and seek the authentic fruit.
The three characteristics of giving are as can be seen in the text.
Treatise:
What is the practice that leads to the arising of delusion and the incurrence of transgression? Commentary:
This section clarifies the characteristics of the three types of precepts.
Regarding the phrase "not stealing,
etc.," this is based on the lay practitioner to demonstrate the inclusion of the ethical discipline of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*),
as it prevents laypeople from committing many evil deeds.
Regarding the phrase "if one is a renunciant" and so forth:
this explains the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*) based on the state of renunciation,
because it involves abandoning all evils and encouraging progress toward the good.
Regarding the passage "Having protected them," this also refers to the precept of gathering sentient beings through renunciation;
for it is the protection of compassion that prevents others from falling into evil.
Treatise:
How does one practice until reaching the dharmas of suffering, pleasure, and so forth? Commentary:
This passage clarifies two types of patience (*kṣānti*).
One should endure the provocations of others without harboring a desire for retaliation;
this is the patience of enduring enmity and harm.
"Furthermore, one should endure gain and loss, etc. refers to the patience of accepting suffering with equanimity (*duḥkhādhivāsana-kṣānti*).
"Honor and sustenance" refers to fame and profit (*yaśas-lābha*).
To encroach upon and damage another's reputation is called decline;
to falsely accuse another is called defamation;
to surpass others in praise is called renown.
To be weighed down by desire is called "craving";
to be truly burdened by it is called "reproach";
to be oppressed by it is called "suffering."
That which accords with one's wishes is called "pleasure.
These environments of opposition and conformity are known as the eight winds;
they can disturb the practitioner, causing them to falsely give rise to joy and anger.
If one abides in equanimity and discerns suchness,
even when encountering affliction from others, one harbors no intent for retaliation;
though encountering the eight winds, the mind remains unmoved.
Since the two types of patience are established through thorough investigation,
this also demonstrates that there are three types of patience.
Treatise:
"How does one practice so as to swiftly become free from all suffering?
[The commentary] states: This passage reveals three types of diligence.
Regarding "not retreating from various virtuous deeds," etc.:
Regarding "armor-like diligence":
it is so called because, like donning armor in the world, one does not retreat or become disheartened.
As for the phrase "one should reflect upon the distant past," etc.:
Vigor that gathers what is wholesome:
because it causes one to remember past empty sufferings so as to exert oneself in what is wholesome;
and that which swiftly brings about the separation from suffering for the sake of benefiting oneself and others.
Diligence for the benefit and happiness [of others].
This is because one exerts diligence oneself out of the desire to liberate others from suffering.
Treatise.
Furthermore, if a person encounters many obstacles... [The commentary states:
Next follows the second section, the expedient means for removing obstacles.
Within this, there are two parts.
First the obstruction,
then the remedy;
this is the first [section].
"Those who have many grave offenses from previous lives" refers to the karmic obstructions that serve as internal causes.
"Those tormented and disturbed by demons, ghosts, and the suffering of illness" refers to external conditions.
This refers to the karmic obstruction resulting from being afflicted by external conditions.
"Being entangled in worldly affairs" reveals the afflictive obstructions that have arisen.
Treatise:
Therefore, one should [cultivate] so that the roots of goodness increase. Commentary:
This explains the method for overcoming hindrances.
Therefore, one should perform prostrations and so forth;
this collectively clarifies the skillful means for removing obstacles.
It is like a person with debts who seeks protection by relying upon a king.
In such a case, one can do nothing against the creditor.
Likewise, when a practitioner prostrates to the Buddhas,
they are protected by the Buddhas and are able to be liberated from all obstacles.
Regarding "confession" and so forth:
this reveals the specific methods for removing the four obstacles.
The obstacle of various evil karmas is removed through confession.
Slandering the true Dharma is countered by exhorting others to eliminate it;
envy for the excellence of others is countered by sympathetic joy;
and attachment to the three realms of existence is countered by dedication.
"Constantly without ceasing or abandoning, one attains exemption from all hindrances," etc.
This concludes the preceding section on the preparatory means for attaining exemption from hindrances and generating wholesome states.
Commentary.
"How does one practice the gates of śamatha and vipaśyanā? Commentary:
The following clarifies śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Within this, there are two parts.
First the question,
then the explanation of its characteristics;
this is the first part.
Treatise:
That which is called "stopping" (śamatha) refers to the meaning of "insight" (vipaśyanā).
Commentary: Below, the characteristics are explained.
The text consists of two parts:
first, a brief clarification;
second, an extensive exposition.
Within the brief [explanation] there are also two parts:
first, citing individual cultivation to clarify conformity;
second, citing the simultaneous integration of both to explain the meaning of conformity.
This is the first [point].
Regarding the phrase "stopping all marks of objective spheres":
it refers to the prior conceptualization that constructs various external objects.
Now, by means of the wisdom of awakening and the principle of consciousness-only, one destroys the appearances of external objects.
Once these appearances cease,
there is nothing to be discriminated.
Therefore, it is called "stopping" (śamatha).
Regarding the analysis of the characteristics of arising and ceasing through causes and conditions:
first, due to the practice of stopping, the mind becomes sunken.
Now, because one observes the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of causes and conditions through awakened wisdom, thereby giving rise to sublime knowledge,
it is called "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*). Regarding the phrase "in accordance with the meaning of *śamatha* contemplation," the Sanskrit term for *śamatha* is *śamatha*.
"Śamatha" is translated here as "calming," and "vipaśyanā" is translated as "contemplation.
The translator of this treatise did so for the sake of providing both the preliminary means and the actual calming and contemplation.
In this context, these are added as being in conformity with śamatha and so forth;
that is to say, the term "brahman" is retained for the skillful means,
while it serves as a metaphorical expression for correct śamatha and vipaśyanā.
That which is precisely śamatha and vipaśyanā is called "contemplation" (vipaśyanā),
because at the time they are practiced in union, it is right contemplation.
If, in this text...
All of these should be translated into Chinese as "conforming to the meaning of śamatha-vipaśyanā" and "conforming to the meaning of vipaśyanā-vipaśyanā."
This means that at the time of skillful means, the cessation of all signs of sensory objects (*nimitta*) is the *śamatha* that accords with correct contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
Therefore, it is said to have the meaning of being "concordant with *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Furthermore, it is because one is able to discern the characteristics of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Because it is an observation that accords with correct contemplation,
it is said to have the meaning of "conformable observation.
Treatise.
"How is it that they accord with [the goal] until both appear simultaneously? The commentary states:
This clarifies the meaning of "concordance" (anuloma) by way of the simultaneous union (yuganaddha).
Regarding the phrase "gradually practicing these two meanings":
This reveals the skillful means that accord with [the goal].
"Appearing simultaneously without being separated" clarifies the correct contemplation that is so accorded.
That is, when one is in cessation, there is contemplation; when one is in contemplation, there is cessation.
When cessation and contemplation are equal and balanced, they are called "inseparable and equal.
Treatise.
"If one cultivates *śamatha*, one sits upright with the mind set correctly. Commentary:
Next, the second section below extensively explains *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Within this, there are two parts.
First, the individual cultivation is clarified;
later, the simultaneous union is revealed.
Within the individual cultivation, there are three parts.
First, one practices calming (*śamatha*);
afterwards, one practices insight (*vipaśyanā*).
Within calming, there are five [aspects].
First, the method for cultivating *śamatha*;
second, the manifest excellence of *śamatha*;
third, the discernment of demonic obstacles to *śamatha*.
Fourth, distinguishing between the true and the false regarding cessation;
fifth, exhorting the cultivation of the desire for cessation.
Regarding the first [of these two], there are two parts.
The first part clarifies that superior persons are able to enter [the path], while the latter reveals that those with obstacles cannot advance; within this, there are also two sections.
First, relying on tranquility, one settles the mind and cultivates the skillful means of *śamatha*.
The latter section consists of three parts: achieving śamatha, attaining meditative concentration, and eliminating hindrances so as not to regress.
Within the first of these, there are two further divisions;
the first clarifies the sequential stages of cultivating śamatha.
This is the first [point].
One who dwells in a secluded place cultivates the object of *śamatha*.
To speak in full,
there should be five conditions:
dwelling in a secluded and quiet place.
Their precepts are pure;
they have an abundance of clothing and food;
and they encounter virtuous friends.
Ceasing all worldly affairs,
I shall now briefly cite the beginning by stating that one dwells in a place of stillness.
As for the term "sitting upright":
This clarifies the regulation of the body:
if the body leans back or is bent forward.
Now, as they dwell by one's side,
having already given rise to indolence and arrogance,
they further induce昏沉 (sloth and torpor).
Therefore, he straightens his body and sits in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).
As for the phrase "rectifying the mind," this reveals the disciplining of the mind.
In this degenerate age, those practitioners who possess right aspiration are few, while those who seek through deviant means are many;
they feign a demeanor of tranquility while greedily pursuing fame and profit,
for their minds are not at rest.
Since there is no way to attain concentration through other means, one seeks it apart from such [erroneous] pursuits; hence it is called "right intention.
This is intended to cause the mind to correspond with the principle (*li*).
To deliver oneself and others to the unsurpassed path is called "taming the mind.
Treatise.
"Not relying on inhalation and exhalation, up to seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing. Commentary:
From here below is the second section, the sequence for cultivating *śamatha* (calm abiding).
Within this, there are two parts.
First, one cultivates śamatha while seated;
subsequently, it also arises during other activities.
Within the former [seated practice], there are also three stages.
First, the mind is separated from the objects of perversion;
subsequently, forgetfulness is eliminated—
this is the first [stage].
What is called "breath" refers to the observed object (*ālambana*).
What is called "form and color" refers to the four types of characteristics—blue, yellow, red, and white—such as the skeletal remains and so forth.
The five universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*), such as earth, water, space, and so on, are all objective spheres that take emptiness as their focal point.
Seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing are the ten *kṛtsnāyatana*s (bases of totality) of consciousness.
Together with the preceding [four], these manifest the ten *kṛtsnāyatana*s.
By investigating and thoroughly comprehending these various objects, one realizes they are merely one's own mind and no longer relies upon external conditions.
Therefore, it is said: "The Treatise states:

'All conceptualizations, up to and including every moment of thought, do not perish. Commentary: This means that all mental constructions, from the most subtle to the most immediate, are subject to cessation without exception.
This is the departure from inverted states of mind.
As for "removing all perceptions and recollections," this refers to the removal of internal conceptual thoughts.
Although one has previously been instructed to abandon the grasping at the characteristics of inverted objects,
if the internal mind still persists, it too is a false inversion.
Therefore, all conceptualizations of the internal mind and every thought that arises must be eliminated.
"Furthermore, 'dispelling perceptions' refers to dispelling the deluded conceptualizations of the subject who perceives.
Previously, it was taught that by abandoning discursive thought, all perceptions are eliminated."
It does not mean that there exists a notion of "removal";
if the notion of removal persists, one has likewise not yet transcended characteristics.
Therefore, even the notion of "removal" must be dispelled.
By means of all these [preceding] lower [explanations], one also eliminates both the agent and the object;
for all phenomena are fundamentally without conceptualization, as they lack a substantial nature that arises and ceases moment by moment.
Since the very conceptualizations to be eliminated cannot be apprehended, [they are likewise abandoned].
How could one further maintain a thought capable of eliminating [other] thoughts?
The treatise states:
"Nor can one follow the mind to the point of using the mind to eliminate the mind. The commentary says:
Next follows the third [section], which eliminates the mind of forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*).
Within this, there are two parts;
first, the prohibition of improper mental application (*ayoniśomanasikāra*).
This is the first [section] showing the skillful means for removal.
Regarding "one must not follow the mind to dwell on external objects":
This prevents the arising of external signs of forgetfulness;
that is to say, one who cultivates *śamatha* must constantly maintain mental attention (*manasikāra*).
How could it be otherwise than merely avoiding inverted objects?
The inverted mind likewise does not abide in the mind that has lost mindfulness regarding external objects.
As for "later using the mind to eliminate the mind," this causes the internal signs of lost mindfulness not to arise.
The preceding mind loses mindfulness;
when it is attached to an object, it has already abandoned that object.
The subsequent mind also loses mindfulness.
To fix the mind upon the inner heart is,
by means of *śamatha*, to eliminate the mind.
Treatise.
"If the mind wanders, it should be brought to abide in right mindfulness. Commentary:
Next, the following passage shows the skillful means for removing [distraction] through right mindfulness.
This section contains two parts.
First, one is caused to abide in right mindfulness;
subsequently, the characteristics of right mindfulness are shown.
This is the first [point].
Although it was previously prescribed that one must not lose mindfulness,
if at some time mindfulness is lost, how should one collect and maintain it?
Therefore, this is shown to cause one to collect and abide in right mindfulness.
This right mindfulness is precisely non-mindfulness.
If one does not give rise to thoughts, they will not wander or disperse on their own.
Therefore, it is said that whenever the mind scatters, one should immediately collect it back.
This does not mean that one gathers a distracted mind by means of the mind;
rather, it is because one gathers the mind with the mind such that the mind does not cease.
Upon reaching this stage where there is no thought and no distraction, it is called abiding in right mindfulness.
There is nothing else to abide in;
for if there were anything to abide in, it would be called wrong mindfulness.
Treatise.
"This one of right mindfulness reaches the point where thought-moment after thought-moment is unattainable. Commentary:
This demonstrates the characteristic of right mindfulness.

It means that by being free from the two characteristics of the grasped (object) and the grasper (subject), the mind has nothing to be attained, thereby realizing and attesting to True Suchness (*tathatā*).
This is the characteristic of right mindfulness.
"One should know that there is only mind and no external objects" indicates that right mindfulness is free from the characteristics of the grasped (the object).
"Furthermore, this very mind is also without equality," etc.,
reveals that right mindfulness is free from the characteristic of the grasper;
being free from the characteristics of both [grasped and grasper], it is entirely without anything to be recollected, thereby realizing and attesting to the source of the mind.
This is called "abiding.
The *Śāstra* says:
"If one rises from one's seat and proceeds to contemplation in accordance [with the teachings]. The *Vyākhyā* states:
This indicates that one also cultivates calm abiding during other activities,
not only while sitting; one should constantly cultivate this calm abiding at all times.
In all other modes of conduct, one should constantly contemplate skillful means,
remaining in accordance with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and the principle of immovability.
Treatise.
"Having practiced for a long time until it is thoroughly matured, one swiftly achieves non-retrogression. The commentary states:
"This refers to the superior person who, among those capable of entry, attains meditative concentration (*samādhi*), eliminates hindrances, and does not regress.
'Having practiced for a long time until it is thoroughly matured, their mind abides,' and so forth."
This clarifies that through the perfection of *śamatha*, one enters the stage of realization.
Regarding the phrase "profoundly subduing the afflictions and [cultivating] faith," this demonstrates the attainment of the stage of entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The text is easy to understand;
there is no need for further explanation.
Treatise:
"Except for those who harbor doubt, it is that which they cannot enter. Commentary:
The preceding section has already revealed the person capable of entering;
this section reveals that which those possessed of obstacles cannot enter.
In this context, seven types of persons who constitute obstacles are enumerated.
First is the one who harbors doubt,
for such a person is an ordinary fool who entertains hesitation.
Second, those who lack faith,
because icchantikas have no aspiration.
Third, those who slander.
Because non-Buddhists give rise to false views;
because those who commit the four grave offenses and those who commit the ten evil deeds have impure minds.
The five karmic obstructions refer to those who have committed the five heinous crimes, for their minds are extremely evil.
The sixth is the pride of self-conceit.
Because those who are self-exalting do not submit to study;
seventh, the indolent,
because the minds of the heedless are unrestrained and dissolute.
If one possesses any one of these seven [obstacles], one will be unable to enter.
Treatise:
Furthermore, based on this, there is the *ekavyūha-samādhi*. Commentary:
Next follows the second [section], the superior capacity for cultivating śamatha.
This contains two parts.
First, it reveals that samādhi has the capacity to know the true meaning.
This is the first [section] of the subsequent revelation of the samādhi that is the basis of the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Regarding the phrase "By means of this samādhi, one immediately knows," etc.:
First, the establishment of the characteristic of supreme capacity refers to its essence.
This means that "all" and so forth below clarify its meaning;
it explains the term *dharmadhātu* as the Buddha-dharmakāya being identical with the bodies of sentient beings.
Because all are the differentiated dharmas known by the mind, they are equal and non-dual; this explains the character "one" (eka) in "one aspect" (ekalakṣaṇa).
Since ordinary beings and sages share the same reality and possess no dual essence, the passage beginning with "is named" (nāma) clarifies the establishment of its name.
This explains the character "knowing.
That which can know the single characteristic of all phenomena within the mind is precisely what is called the *ekavyūha-samādhi*.
The first refers to suchness,
which is the object of this samādhi;
"practice" refers to the practice of understanding.
This is the samādhi.
Entering this samādhi, one fully knows that the dharma-realm of all Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, is characterized by non-differentiation.
Treatise.
"One should know that True Suchness extends to the immeasurable samādhis. Commentary:
This reveals that True Suchness is the foundation of samādhi;
that is to say, this True Suchness is the essence of samādhi.
Samādhi is precisely the functioning of True Suchness (tathatā).
Because all samādhis arise in accordance with True Suchness,
True Suchness is said to be the root of samādhi.
If a person practices the samādhi of true suchness (tathatā), they will be able to gradually give rise to the immeasurable;
this is because they correctly contemplate the essence of true suchness.
Treatise.
"Or there may be sentient beings who arrive at the marks of male, female, and so forth. Commentary:
Next, the third section below distinguishes the cessation of demonic activities (*māra-karman*).
This contains two parts.
First, the brief;
second, the detailed.
Within the brief, there are further two parts.
First the obstruction,
then the remedy;
this is the first.
Regarding the statement that sentient beings lack the power of roots of goodness,
this cites the cause of the obstacle;
it means they lack superior, preeminent roots of goodness, not that they are entirely devoid of them.
The following passage clarifies that which acts as an obstacle.
"Māra" refers to the celestial Māra;
by nature he delights in birth and death, fearing that others might escape his realm.
Faults are remedied through cessation.
"Ghosts" refers to the *duīchǎng* ghosts;
"spirits" refers to the *jìngmèi* spirits.
Because they fall into these categories by practicing false paths,
they are collectively termed "non-Buddhists" (tīrthika).
Ghosts and spirits harbor hatred and jealousy toward such practitioners and also obstruct their cultivation of śamatha.
Alternatively, the following describes the characteristics of their affliction:
as with the three preceding categories, they are all capable of causing strange transformations,
or they manifest evil forms to terrify the mind.
Sometimes they manifest beautiful forms to delude their minds;
sometimes they manifest various appearances to divert their singular focus.
Therefore, it is said that within the assembly, they manifest terrors and the like.
Treatise:
One should maintain the mindfulness that "it is but mind," until finally no affliction arises.
Commentary: This briefly explains the method of cultivation.
If all objects are merely one's own mind,
how much more so the objects within meditative concentration? Therefore,
one should investigate the principle that all is mind-only.
The objects of affliction extinguish themselves and cannot cause disturbance,
for all demonic realms arise based on moving thoughts;
one observes that these are merely mind, as they are not known by those [demons].
Treatise:
Or manifesting in the form of a celestial deity—this is true *nirvāṇa*. Commentary:
Hereafter, the various distinctions of demonic activities (*mārakarma*) will be extensively analyzed.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the identification of demonic activities;
second, the revelation of their remedies.
The beginning and middle clarify five pairs;
this is the first, the pair of manifested forms and sounds.
Because these manifested forms and methods of teaching differ from the [true] characteristics, they may confuse practitioners and cause them to lose their original path.
Therefore, all these are termed demonic obstacles (*māra-antarāya*).
The treatise states:
"Or it causes people to become aware of matters concerning fame and profit. The commentary says:
This second attainment is the general exposition of the supernormal powers;
by knowing past lives and so forth,

Next, the specific characteristics of the benefits of the three types of wisdom are revealed.
This section contains three parts, namely:
hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
This is the first point.
True Suchness and original enlightenment are identical to those of the Buddhas;
in a single thought-moment of realization, one is no different from the Buddhas.
One who practices with joy and without timidity should be known as one who will certainly succeed to the lineage of the Buddhas;
the Buddha will grant them a prediction of enlightenment.
This is certain and beyond doubt.
Treatise:
Suppose there were a person who was beyond all comparison. Commentary: [As stated above.]
This is the benefit of wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī prajñā*).
Although the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*) involve much [effort], they are not the untainted karma (*anāsravakarma*);
although the treatises on reflection involve little [effort], they are the cause for the Buddha’s untainted [wisdom].
For this reason, it surpasses what came before and cannot be illustrated by analogy.
Treatise:
Furthermore, if a person reaches the limit of non-existence... Commentary says:
This clarifies the benefit of cultivating wisdom.
The phrase "if a person" and so forth indicates that although the time is brief, the merit is great.
"Suppose that... and so forth refers to the characteristics of a great measure.
"For what reason... and so forth explains the reason for its being great.
This refers to the principle of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) elucidated in this treatise.
The essence of nature is boundless,
and its virtues are likewise inexhaustible.
Those who give rise to cultivated wisdom accord with and conform to these innate virtues.
The merit is boundless and no one can exhaust it.
Treatise:
There are sentient beings who undergo great suffering and affliction. Commentary: There are sentient beings who undergo great suffering and affliction. Commentary:
Next, the following section reveals the gravity of the offense of slandering [the Dharma].
Within this, there are four parts.
First, the demonstration that such slander constitutes a grave offense.
Second, admonishing and exhorting to cease slander;
third, explaining the meaning of the gravity of the offense;
fourth, further explaining the underlying reasons.
This is the first case.
Those who commit the five heinous crimes suffer for only five kalpas;
however, those who slander this treatise shall undergo the ultimate suffering of the Avīci hell throughout the ten directions for immeasurable kalpas.
This is because it is the Dharma that is the mother of all Buddhas.
Treatise:
Therefore, sentient beings should not disparage it. Commentary: [As stated above.]
This is an exhortation against the mind of slander.
Because one incurs great sin through such defamation,
even if one has never heard [this teaching], it is unfit for thought or cultivation.
One should simply have faith in it from above;
one should not revile it.
Thus says the treatise.
"By deeply harming oneself, one harms the seeds of the Triple Gem. The commentary states:
This explains the gravity of the offense.
Those who commit the five heinous crimes merely harm themselves.
It is not that the Three Jewels are severed,
nor is it a profound harm;
yet how could those who slander this Dharma avoid falling into the great realms of suffering for both themselves and others?
They also sever the seeds of the Triple Gem for both themselves and others;
this is called deeply harming oneself and harming others,
for they cut off all seeds of the Triple Gem.
Treatise:
Because all Tathāgatas enter into the Buddha-wisdom. Commentary:
The following section further explains the meaning of severing [the continuity of] the Three Jewels.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, it clarifies that the Jewel of the Buddha is established in dependence upon the Dharma;
second, it reveals that the Jewel of the Sangha exists in dependence upon the Dharma.
This is the first [point].
Regarding the statement that the Tathāgata attains nirvāṇa by relying on this:
it clarifies that past and present Buddhas achieve fruition based on the Dharma as their cause.
Regarding the statement that "Bodhisattvas enter the wisdom of a Buddha by means of cultivation," this reveals that future Buddhas take the Dharma as their cause; therefore,
those who slander the Dharma sever the lineage of the Buddhas.
Treatise:
It should be understood that the attainment of the past constitutes pure faith. Commentary:
This demonstrates that the Jewel of the Sangha is established in dependence upon the Dharma.
Now, as for the term "Saṃgha," its meaning is harmony and union.
Only when there is pure faith and no transgression can one be called a Saṃgha.
Since the Bodhisattvas of the three periods have attained pure faith by relying on this Dharma,
to slander this Dharma is likewise called severing the Sangha Jewel.
Because the Buddha and the Sangha are severed, the Dharma also does not prevail.
Therefore, this is called severing the Three Jewels.
Treatise:
For this reason, sentient beings should diligently practice and study. Commentary: [As stated above].
The preceding section has already clarified the benefits and harms resulting from faith and slander;
this concludes the third point, which is an exhortation to practice.
This is because those who engage in such slander bring great harm upon themselves and others.
Sentient beings who desire to seek their own benefit and the benefit of others, and to achieve great purpose, should diligently study and practice this treatise.
Treatise:
The profoundness of all Buddhas extends to the realm of all sentient beings. Commentary: This means that the profound nature of all Buddhas reaches throughout the entire domain of sentient beings.
What has been presented above has already clarified the main body of the Dharma-gift;
this section clarifies the dedication and dissemination.
Within the text, there are four phrases.
This single verse is composed to manifest the principles, teachings, practices, and fruits of the Mahāyāna.
The first line specifically manifests the Dharma that is expounded, namely, the Mahāyāna principles upon which the exposition relies.
This means that this very single mind is what the Buddha has realized;
it encompasses two gates.
That these are not differentiated by fixed limits is called the meaning of profundity.
The first phrase signifies the meaning of "vastness," as it encompasses the three great [vehicles] and functions everywhere.
The second phrase precisely reveals the expressive text itself:
the Mahāyāna teachings arising from the principle.
In accordance with the principles revealed by the measure of my own wisdom,
I have composed this Mahāyāna teaching of dhāraṇī, condensing manifold meanings into concise words.
The next phrase correctly reveals the bestowing of blessings upon all sentient beings;
it manifests the vows and practices of the Mahāyāna.
This means that, just as the Dharma-nature reaches everywhere, [so too does this compassion].
My merit in establishing this teaching based on principle is likewise like the Dharma-nature bestowing upon all sentient beings.
The latter phrase correctly reveals the benefit of bestowing blessings;
it reveals the fruit and advantage obtained through reliance on practice and vows.
It causes all sentient beings universally to attain the benefits of the fruit of the Mahāyāna.
